Finding roots numerically

Most equations met in engineering — cos⁡x=x, x5−3x+1=0, friction-factor and heat-transfer equations — have no formula for their solutions. Numerical root finders produce a sequence of approximations that closes in on a solution of f(x)=0. This calculator implements the two classic methods and shows every iteration, so you can see how — and whether — they converge.

Try changing the input

Solve x2−2=0 with both methods to the same tolerance. Bisection needs about 20 steps; Newton's method needs 5, because its number of correct digits roughly doubles each step.

Methods and convergence

Bisection
Start with [a,b] where f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs. Evaluate f at the midpoint m=a+b2 and keep the half that still contains a sign change. The error after k steps is at most b−a2k: slow but guaranteed for continuous f.
Newton–Raphson
xk+1=xk−f(xk)f′(xk). Very fast (quadratic convergence) near a simple root, but it needs a good starting guess and can fail: if f′(xk)=0 the tangent is horizontal; the iterates may cycle (as for x3−2x+2 from 0) or diverge.

Stopping rule: stop when successive approximations differ by less than the tolerance (and ∣f(x)∣ is small), or when the iteration limit is reached — in which case the calculator reports non-convergence rather than an unreliable number.

Worked example

Solve cos⁡x=x with Newton's method from x0=1

Step 1 — Set up

f(x)=cos⁡x−x,f′(x)=−sin⁡x−1

Step 2 — First iteration

x1=1−cos⁡1−1−sin⁡1−1≈1−−0.4597−1.8415≈0.7504

Step 3 — Continue

x2≈0.739113, x3≈0.739085; after 5 iterations x≈0.7390851332.

Assumptions and limits

  • f must be continuous on the bisection interval; Newton's method also needs f to be differentiable (the derivative is computed symbolically).
  • Tolerance between 10−4 and 10−10; at most 1000 iterations.
  • Each method finds one root. To find others, change the interval or the starting guess — the graph shows where the curve crosses the axis.
